decisions.rationale: The retained Scanlon et al. (2012) primary article explicitly reports approximately 330 km³ of High Plains groundwater depletion from predevelopment in the 1950s through 2007 using groundwater-level data from 3,600 wells. The exact supporting quotation and offsets match the immutable capture. The statement, label, claim kind, Earth-sciences domain and geographic identity are consistent with the evidence. Reported attributes the estimate to its source; undated and frontier=false make no additional chronology or currency claims. No relationship or taxonomy placement is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The estimate converts groundwater-level observations into storage changes using aquifer properties and assumptions. It is not a direct volumetric measurement, does not span a GRACE-matched observation period and cannot independently demonstrate agreement with satellite estimates. Geographic averaging conceals substantial regional variation. The supporting article also cites an earlier USGS investigation, so this publication is not an independent replication of that underlying well analysis.

decisions.rationale: The retained Scanlon et al. passage explicitly reports about 330 km³ depletion in the High Plains, inferred from groundwater levels in 3,600 wells between predevelopment (about the 1950s) and 2007. The candidate attributes the estimate and preserves measurement method, geography, period, and units. Claim/earth and distinct identity are reasonable; reported/undated/frontier=false are neutral. No edge, direction, or taxonomy placement is asserted.
decisions.limitations: Well levels require conversion to aquifer storage, including spatial and specific-yield assumptions. The 1950s–2007 period cannot independently validate GRACE observations from different periods.

decisions.rationale: The captured Scanlon et al. article explicitly provides an approximately 140 km³ historical Central Valley estimate from groundwater models, separating 60 km³ for the 1860s through 1961 and 80 km³ for 1962 through 2003. Both periods and quantities match the candidate. Exact quotation and offsets are valid. The representation correctly identifies a model-derived reported claim within Earth sciences, with neutral chronology and frontier metadata and no proposed relationship or placement.
decisions.limitations: These are historical model estimates, not independent satellite measurements. The 140 km³ figure is an aggregate of estimates covering different periods and potentially different model formulations. Spatially heterogeneous depletion and intervening recovery cannot be inferred from the cumulative figure alone. Agreement with a GRACE estimate from another period would not constitute temporally matched validation.

decisions.rationale: The Scanlon et al. text explicitly gives an approximately 140 km³ model-based Central Valley historical depletion estimate, split into 60 km³ from the 1860s to 1961 and 80 km³ from 1962 to 2003. The candidate retains attribution, modeled basis, periods and units. Claim/earth, distinct identity, and neutral metadata fit; no relation or placement is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The numbers are historical model estimates, not satellite measurements. Model calibration, water-budget assumptions, and uncertainties are not quantified in the retained quotation.

decisions.rationale: The source explicitly states that GRACE measures changes in total water storage and describes estimating groundwater changes by subtracting snow-water-equivalent storage, reservoir surface-water storage and modeled soil-moisture storage. The supplied exact excerpt and Unicode offsets are valid. The candidate faithfully describes the particular residual method used in the cited research rather than asserting that satellite gravity directly isolates groundwater. Its claim kind, Earth domain and neutral metadata are appropriate; no edges or placements require evaluation.
decisions.limitations: The enumerated subtractions reflect the cited methodology and are not a universally exhaustive inventory of terrestrial water compartments. Depending on region and methodology, vegetation water, other surface-water bodies and additional terms can matter. Uncertainty in auxiliary products propagates into groundwater estimates. Satellite observations and groundwater residuals must not be treated as equivalent independent measurements.

decisions.rationale: The exact retained passage says GRACE observes total water-storage changes and groundwater is estimated by subtracting changes in snow, reservoir surface water, and modeled soil moisture. The candidate states this specific residual-inference procedure without claiming direct groundwater sensing. Kind/domain, identity, and neutral metadata are appropriate; no directed relationship is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The source does not quantify subtraction uncertainty, unmodeled storage components, or suitability in all regions. The description is specific to the approach reported by Scanlon et al.

decisions.rationale: Scanlon et al. explicitly report correlations between GRACE-derived groundwater-storage changes and estimates derived from approximately 1,000 High Plains monitoring wells, with r² values from 0.7 to 0.8. The exact quote, numerical range and offsets match the capture. The candidate preserves the measured quantity as r² rather than r and appropriately attributes the comparison to the published study. Kind, domain, identity and neutral metadata are justified. No unsupported relationship direction or taxonomy placement is introduced.
decisions.limitations: The retained passage cites earlier comparison studies, making this a report of published comparisons rather than a newly established independent replication. It does not specify the compared time series, spatial masks, regression details, confidence intervals or possible common modeling inputs. Correlation does not establish agreement in absolute groundwater volume, unbiased trend magnitude or complete measurement independence. Additional original-method evidence is required before concluding that the two methods independently establish matching depletion rates.

decisions.rationale: The captured text reports r² of 0.7–0.8 between GRACE-derived storage changes and estimates from monitoring about 1,000 High Plains wells. The candidate uses r² rather than r, preserves geographic and methodological scope, and attributes the comparison. Claim/earth, independent candidate identity, neutral metadata, and absence of graph edges are justified.
decisions.limitations: The retained passage gives no common-period details or uncertainty bounds. Correlation alone cannot prove equality of absolute groundwater depletion, measurement independence, or agreement across all aquifer subregions.

decisions.rationale: The retained article explicitly reports GRACE-derived Central Valley groundwater depletion of 6–8 km³ per year and 24–34 km³ over April 2006 through March 2010. The candidate reproduces the source's values, units, geography and dates without presenting the residual estimate as a direct aquifer-only observation. The exact quotation and offsets match. The claim representation and neutral metadata are justified, with no proposed relationships or placement.
decisions.limitations: The source's approximate rate and total ranges should not be treated as exact mathematical identities or uncertainty intervals without inspecting the underlying analyses. GRACE-based groundwater estimates depend on subtracting other terrestrial water-storage components. The paper compares this drought with earlier modeled droughts, not necessarily with independent measurements for the same four-year period. The cited values therefore cannot by themselves establish direct satellite-well agreement.

decisions.rationale: Scanlon et al. explicitly report GRACE-derived Central Valley groundwater depletion of 6–8 km³/year and 24–34 km³ total during April 2006–March 2010. Claim/earth, unique identity and neutral metadata are appropriate; no relationship or placement is proposed.

decisions.rationale: The USGS primary report explicitly estimates approximately 2.91 billion acre-feet of recoverable High Plains groundwater in 2019 and a decline of 286.4 million acre-feet, about 10%, relative to predevelopment. The supplied quotation matches the retained source at its stated offsets. The proposed claim preserves recoverable storage, the geographic scope and the distinction between the 2019 stock and historical change. Source attribution, Earth-sciences classification and neutral metadata are justified. No relationships or taxonomy placements are proposed.
decisions.limitations: Recoverable groundwater storage is calculated from mapped saturated thickness and assigned specific yield, not measured directly as one volume. The 10% change is an aquifer-wide estimate and masks substantial state-level differences. It should not be numerically reconciled with earlier estimates in cubic kilometers without aligning aquifer boundaries, periods, conversion assumptions and definitions of recoverable storage. This source does not independently validate a GRACE groundwater time series.

decisions.rationale: The retained USGS report explicitly gives about 2.91 billion acre-feet of recoverable High Plains storage in 2019 and a predevelopment-to-2019 decline of about 286.4 million acre-feet (about 10%). Neutral metadata, claim/earth and distinct identity are justified; no edge or placement is inferred.
decisions.limitations: These are USGS estimated recoverable storage quantities, contingent on mapped groundwater levels, saturated thickness and specific yield; they are not GRACE-only observations.

decisions.rationale: Two distinct exact excerpts from the retained USGS report support both components: an aquifer-wide area-weighted mean water-level rise of 0.1 foot from 2017 to 2019 and an estimated 1.6 million acre-foot increase in recoverable storage over the same interval. Both quotations and their offsets match. The candidate distinguishes groundwater levels from derived groundwater storage and limits the increase to 2017–2019. Claim kind, Earth domain and neutral metadata are justified; no edges or placements are proposed.
decisions.limitations: The 0.1-foot figure is an area-weighted average, not a rise at every monitoring well. The reported increase is a model-assisted regional storage estimate. Texas experienced declines while Nebraska experienced increases, so describing this interval as uniform aquifer recovery would be incorrect. Short-term net gain does not reverse cumulative depletion since predevelopment. The result is not a GRACE comparison and provides no independent satellite corroboration.

decisions.rationale: Two unique exact passages in the USGS capture separately establish a 0.1-foot area-weighted aquifer-average water-level rise and an overall 1.6-million-acre-foot recoverable-storage increase during 2017–2019. The candidate combines these simultaneous results without claiming every locality recovered. Claim/earth, distinct identity, neutral metadata, and absence of edges are justified.
decisions.limitations: The short-term net rise does not reverse long-term depletion. The estimates are based on well observations and conversion assumptions, with regional differences and uncertainty not fully represented in these excerpts.

decisions.rationale: The retained USGS report explicitly identifies an aquifer-wide area-weighted average specific yield of 15.1%, excluding areas of little or no saturated thickness, and state-level averages ranging from 8.1% in Wyoming to 18.5% in Oklahoma. The exact excerpt and offsets match. The candidate correctly represents these as specific-yield assumptions used for groundwater-storage estimation, rather than observed depletion percentages. The Earth domain, claim kind, identity and neutral status, era and frontier metadata are justified. No relationships or placement are proposed.
decisions.limitations: These values derive from spatially assigned specific-yield ranges and averaging methods; they are not independently measured uniform physical properties. Specific yield varies across sediment types and locations. Storage estimates can be sensitive to these assumptions, and the reported range of state averages does not describe the full range of local specific yields. The result should not be treated as direct evidence of satellite accuracy.

decisions.rationale: The exact USGS passage states 15.1% area-weighted aquifer-average specific yield excluding little/no saturated-thickness areas, with state averages ranging from 8.1% in Wyoming to 18.5% in Oklahoma. decisions.rationale: The captured NASA JPL product description expressly reports 4,551 relatively independent surface-mass estimates derived using an equal-area 3-degree mascon grid and mapped to a regular 0.5-degree latitude-longitude grid. canonical_record.label: sort
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines sort as: Arrange items in a predetermined order. There are dozens of algorithms, the choice of which depends on factors such as the number of items relative to working memory, knowledge of the orderliness of the items or the range of the keys , the cost of comparing keys vs. the cost of moving items, etc. Most algorithms can be implemented as an in-place sort , and many can be implemented so they are stable , too. Formal Definition: The sort operation may be defined in terms of an initial array, S, of N items and a final array, S′, as follows. S′ i ≤ S′ i+1 , 0 < i < N (the items are in order) and S′ is a permutation of S.

canonical_record.label: counting sort
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines counting sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the number of distinct keys is small compared to the number of items. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding keys. The second pass puts each item in its final place according to the auxiliary entry for that key.

canonical_record.label: queue
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines queue as: A collection of items in which only the earliest added item may be accessed. Basic operations are add (to the tail ) or enqueue and delete (from the head ) or dequeue. Delete returns the item removed. Also known as "first-in, first-out" or FIFO. Formal Definition: It is convenient to define delete or dequeue in terms of remove and a new operation, front. The operations new(), add(v, Q), front(Q), and remove(Q) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a queue front(add(v, new())) = v remove(add(v, new())) = new() front(add(v, add(w, Q))) = front(add(w, Q)) remove(add(v, add(w, Q))) = add(v, remove(add(w, Q))) where Q is a queue and v and w are values. Also known as FIFO.

canonical_record.label: stack
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines stack as: A collection of items in which only the most recently added item may be removed. The latest added item is at the top. Basic operations are push and pop. Often top and isEmpty are available, too. Also known as "last-in, first-out" or LIFO. Formal Definition: The operations new(), push(v, S), top(S), and popoff(S) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a stack popoff(push(v, S)) = S top(push(v, S)) = v where S is a stack and v is a value. The pop operation is a combination of top, to return the top value, and popoff, to remove the top value. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(push(v, S)) = false Also known as LIFO.

canonical_record.label: graph
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines graph as: A set of items connected by edges . Each item is called a vertex or node . Formally, a graph is a set of vertices and a binary relation between vertices, adjacency. Formal Definition: A graph G can be defined as a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph is undirected, the adjacency relation defined by the edges is symmetric , or E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V} (sets of vertices rather than ordered pairs). If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive .

canonical_record.label: Bellman-Ford algorithm
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines Bellman-Ford algorithm as: An efficient algorithm to solve the single-source shortest-path problem . Weights may be negative. The algorithm initializes the distance to the source vertex to 0 and all other vertices to ∞. It then does V-1 passes (V is the number of vertices) over all edges relaxing, or updating, the distance to the destination of each edge. Finally it checks each edge again to detect negative weight cycles , in which case it returns false. The time complexity is O(VE) , where E is the number of edges. Also known as Ford-Bellman.

canonical_record.label: Prim-Jarnik algorithm
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines Prim-Jarnik algorithm as: Compute a minimum spanning tree by beginning with any vertex as the current tree . At each step add a least edge between any vertex not in the tree and any vertex in the tree. Continue until all vertices have been added.

canonical_record.label: divide and conquer
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines divide and conquer as: Solve a problem, either directly because solving that instance is easy (typically, because the instance is small) or by dividing it into two or more smaller instances. Each of these smaller instances is recursively solved, and the solutions are combined to produce a solution for the original instance.

canonical_record.label: backtracking
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines backtracking as: Find a solution by trying one of several choices. If the choice proves incorrect, computation backtracks or restarts at the point of choice and tries another choice. It is often convenient to maintain choice points and alternate choices using recursion .

canonical_record.label: B-tree
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines B-tree as: A balanced search tree in which every node has between ⌈ m/2⌉ and m children , where m>1 is a fixed integer. m is the order . The root may have as few as 2 children. This is a good structure if much of the tree is in slow memory (disk), since the height , and hence the number of accesses, can be kept small, say one or two, by picking a large m. Also known as balanced multiway tree.

canonical_record.label: finite state machine
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines finite state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a set of states , a start state , an input alphabet , and a transition function that maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Computation begins in the start state with an input string. It changes to new states depending on the transition function. There are many variants, for instance, machines having actions (outputs) associated with transitions ( Mealy machine ) or states ( Moore machine ), multiple start states, transitions conditioned on no input symbol (a null) or more than one transition for a given symbol and state ( nondeterministic finite state machine ), one or more states designated as accepting states ( recognizer ), etc. Also known as finite state automaton.

canonical_record.label: priority queue
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines priority queue as: An abstract data type to efficiently support finding the item with the highest priority across a series of operations. The basic operations are: insert, find-minimum (or maximum), and delete-minimum (or maximum). Some implementations also efficiently support join two priority queues ( meld ), delete an arbitrary item, and increase the priority of a item (decrease-key). Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(v, PQ), find-minimum or min(PQ), and delete-minimum or dm(PQ) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a priority queue min(insert(v, new())) = v dm(insert(v, new())) = new() min(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then v else min(insert(w, PQ)) dm(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then insert(w, PQ) else insert(v, dm(insert(w, PQ))) where PQ is a priority queue, v and w are items, and priority(v) is the priority of item v.

canonical_record.label: hash table
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines hash table as: A dictionary in which keys are mapped to array positions by hash functions . Having the keys of more than one item map to the same position is called a collision . There are many collision resolution schemes , but they may be divided into open addressing , chaining , and keeping one special overflow area. Perfect hashing avoids collisions, but may be time-consuming to create. Also known as scatter storage.

canonical_record.label: breadth-first search
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines breadth-first search as: Any search algorithm that considers neighbors of a vertex , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search, before any outgoing edges of the vertex. Extremes are searched last. This is typically implemented with a queue .

canonical_record.label: depth-first search
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines depth-first search as: (1) Any search algorithm that considers outgoing edges ( children ) of a vertex before any of the vertex's siblings , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search. Extremes are searched first. This is easily implemented with recursion . (2) An algorithm that marks all vertices in a directed graph in the order they are discovered and finished, partitioning the graph into a forest . Also known as DFS.

canonical_record.label: directed graph
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines directed graph as: A graph whose edges are ordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge can be followed from one vertex to another vertex. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}. Also known as digraph, oriented graph.

canonical_record.label: array
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines array as: An assemblage of items that are randomly accessible by integers, the index. Formal Definition: Ignoring size an array may be seen as an abstract data type with the operations new(), set(i, v, A), and get(i, A), where i is a numeric index, v is a value, and A is an array. The operations may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns an array get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j Compare this with a dictionary using integers as keys. If the contents of a new array are set to some implicit initial value v i , we could add the following rule for get. get(i, new()) = v i Typically arrays have a fixed size and use either 0-based indexing or 1-based indexing . Fixed initial size and 0-based indexing may incorporated as follows. new(s) returns an array, which has a size s size(new(s)) = s size(set(i, v, A)) = size(A) get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v if 0 ≤ i < size(A) get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j One-based or other indexing may be defined similarly.

new(s) returns an array, which has a size s
size(new(s)) = s

get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v if 0 ≤ i < size(A)
get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j
One-based or other indexing may be defined similarly.

canonical_record.label: set
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines set as: An unordered collection of values where each value occurs at most once. A group of elements with three properties: (1) all elements belong to a universe , (2) either each element is a member of the set or it is not, and (3) the elements are unordered. Formal Definition: As an abstract data type , a set has a single query function, isIn(v, S), which tells whether an element is a member of the set or not, and two modifier functions, add(v, S) and remove(v, S). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a set isIn(v, new()) = false isIn(v, add(v, S)) = true isIn(v, add(u, S)) = isIn(v , S) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, S)) = remove(v, S) remove(v, add(u, S)) = add(u, remove(v, S)) if v ≠ u where S is a set and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, S)) = false

canonical_record.label: tree
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines tree as: (1) A data structure accessed beginning at the root node. Each node is either a leaf or an internal node . An internal node has one or more child nodes and is called the parent of its child nodes. All children of the same node are siblings . Contrary to a physical tree, the root is usually depicted at the top of the structure, and the leaves are depicted at the bottom. (2) A connected , undirected , acyclic graph . It is rooted and ordered unless otherwise specified. Thanks to Joshua O'Madadhain ( [email protected] ) for the figure, 6 October 2005. Formal Definition: (1) A tree is either empty (no nodes), or a root and zero or more subtrees. The subtrees are ordered.

canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect hashing as: A hash function that maps each different key to a distinct integer. Usually all possible keys must be known beforehand. A hash table that uses a perfect hash has no collisions . Formal Definition: A function f is perfect for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k. Also known as optimal hashing.

canonical_record.label: open addressing
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines open addressing as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which all items are stored within the hash table . In case of collision , other positions are computed, giving a probe sequence , and checked until an empty position is found. Some ways of computing possible new positions are less efficient because of clustering . Typically items never move once put in place, but in Robin Hood hashing , LCFS hashing , and other techniques, previously placed items may move.

canonical_record.label: cuckoo hashing
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines cuckoo hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two hash tables , T 1 and T 2 , and two different hash functions , h 1 and h 2 . Each key , k, is either in T 1 [h 1 (k)] or T 2 [h 2 (k)]. A new key , k, is stored in T 1 [h 1 (k)]. If that location is already occupied by another key, l, the other key is moved to T 2 [h 2 (l)]. Keys are moved back and forth until a key moves to an empty location or a limit is reached. If the limit is reached, new hash functions are chosen, and the tables are rehashed. For tables that are a bit less than half full and with carefully chosen universal hashing functions, performance is good. A key is deleted by removing it from a table.

canonical_record.label: Fibonaccian search
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonaccian search as: Search a sorted array by narrowing possible locations to progressively smaller intervals. Begin with two Fibonacci numbers , p (F(n)) and q (F(n+1)), such that p < n ≤ q, where n is the size of the array. The first step checks location p. The size of the next interval is p, if the key is less than the item at that location, or q-p (F(n-1)) if it is greater.

canonical_record.label: Huffman coding
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length character coding based on the frequency of each character. First, each character becomes a one-node binary tree , with the character as the only node . The character's frequency is the tree's frequency. Two trees with the least frequencies are joined as the subtrees of a new root that is assigned the sum of their frequencies. Repeat until all characters are in one tree. One code bit represents each level . Thus more frequent characters are near the root and are coded with few bits, and rare characters are far from the root and are coded with many bits. Also known as static Huffman coding.

On each pass swap pairs of items separated by the increment or gap, if needed, and reduce the gap (divide it by about 1.3). The gap starts at about 3/4 of the number of items. Continue until the gap is 1 and a pass had no swaps.

canonical_record.label: big-O notation
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines big-O notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = O(g(n)) means it is less than some constant multiple of g(n). The notation is read, "f of n is big oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The values of c and k must be fixed for the function f and must not depend on n. Also known as O, asymptotic upper bound.

canonical_record.label: NP-complete
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-complete as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked for correctness, given a certificate , by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input (that is, it is NP ) and no other NP problem is more than a polynomial factor harder. Informally, a problem is NP-complete if answers can be verified quickly, and a quick algorithm to solve this problem can be used to solve all other NP problems quickly.
